question: Why do we have a postnatal referral system in place?

options.A: To reduce the total number of patients visiting government hospitals
options.B: To connect primary clinics with facilities that can handle emergencies
options.C: To collect data for national health research and statistics
options.D: To provide routine immunization schedules for newborns

explanation: Think of a referral system as a bridge! It links small community health posts to advanced hospitals so mothers and babies get rapid help when an emergency hits. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h1)

question: Why are community nurses and midwives often called the 'gatekeepers' of the referral process?

options.A: They approve the financial budget for community health centers
options.B: They are the first to spot complications and decide when to escalate care
options.C: They decide which patients are wealthy enough to afford hospital care
options.D: They physically transport every single patient to the general hospital

explanation: Spotting trouble early is your superpower as a nurse! Because you monitor mums and babies closely, you make that vital first call to transfer them when things go south. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h1)

question: A postnatal mother comes in with a fever and foul-smelling lochia. What does this usually mean?
explanation: Bad-smelling lochia combined with a fever is a classic red flag for a uterine infection. You'll want to escalate this quickly for medical treatment! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h2)

question: A nursing mother complains of painful swelling and redness in only her left calf. What should you do?

options.A: Advise her to apply hot compresses and stay in bed for three days
options.B: Prescribe oral iron supplements for suspected postpartum anaemia
options.C: Reassure her that this is a normal muscular strain from carrying the baby
options.D: Refer her urgently for suspected deep vein thrombosis

explanation: Pain and swelling in just one leg is a warning sign of a blood clot (DVT). It needs an urgent hospital check to keep her safe! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h2)

question: Which set of symptoms in a postpartum mother is a strong warning sign of impending eclampsia (seizures)?

options.A: Severe headache, blurred vision, and upper tummy (epigastric) pain
options.B: Dry mouth, joint stiffness, and mild fatigue
options.C: Frequent urination, extreme thirst, and itchy skin
options.D: Cough, chest pain, and difficulty breathing

explanation: Keep your eyes open for these head and tummy warning signs! They tell you severe pre-eclampsia might be progressing into dangerous seizures. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h3)

question: Why is sudden, heavy postpartum bleeding that causes dizziness treated as a top emergency?

options.A: It prevents the mother from producing enough breast milk
options.B: It quickly leads to hypovolemic shock and organ failure
options.C: It always results in permanent damage to the kidneys
options.D: It causes the baby to reject breastfeeding due to stress

explanation: Rapid blood loss starves vital organs of oxygen. Without fast intervention, the mother's body can slip into shock very quickly. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h3)

question: What temperature reading tells you a newborn baby has hypothermia?
explanation: For a newborn, anything under 36.5°C means they are getting too cold (hypothermia) and need warming up fast! [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h4)

question: A 5-day-old baby is brought in with yellow skin that reaches all the way to the soles of their feet. What is your next step?

options.A: Reassure the mother that yellow skin is completely normal after birth
options.B: Advise the mother to feed the baby more frequently with plain water
options.C: Tell the mother to place the baby under direct sunlight through a glass window
options.D: Arrange an immediate referral for management of severe neonatal jaundice

explanation: When jaundice spreads all the way to the palms and soles, bilirubin levels are dangerously high and need hospital treatment to protect the baby's brain. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h4)

question: What is the main goal of stabilizing a patient at a primary health centre before sending them away?

options.A: To reduce the financial cost of treatment at the main hospital
options.B: To keep the patient alive and as stable as possible during transit
options.C: To completely cure the patient before sending them away
options.D: To avoid paperwork and documentation at the referral hospital

explanation: Stabilization is all about buying time and keeping vital signs steady so the patient can survive the journey to the bigger hospital. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h5)

question: You are preparing a postpartum mother with severe bleeding for emergency transfer. What is an essential step?

options.A: Instructing her to walk to the ambulance to improve circulation
options.B: Securing an intravenous (IV) line and starting fluid resuscitation
options.D: Waiting for blood test results before allowing her to leave

explanation: Getting an IV line running replaces lost fluids and holds her blood pressure steady during the bumpy ride to the hospital. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h5)

question: What crucial information must you always write down in a patient's referral note?

options.A: The religious affiliation and family history of the patient
options.B: A detailed breakdown of transport costs incurred by the family
options.C: The personal phone number of the community health officer
options.D: Vital signs, suspected diagnosis, and treatment given so far

explanation: The receiving doctors need a quick cheat sheet! Always include current vital signs, what you think is wrong, and any drugs or fluids you've already given. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h6)

question: Why is it smart to call the receiving hospital on the phone before sending an emergency patient?

options.A: To confirm the exact home address of the ambulance driver
options.B: To ask the doctor on duty for permission to use their hospital ambulance
options.C: To ensure the receiving team can prepare equipment and space for the patient
options.D: To negotiate the medical bills before the patient arrives at the gate

explanation: A quick heads-up phone call lets the hospital prep a bed, oxygen, or blood products before the ambulance even rolls through their gates. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h6)

question: What is a major financial hurdle that often delays emergency referrals in many communities?

options.A: Excessive availability of free government health insurance
options.B: Mandatory taxes collected at community health gates
options.C: Out-of-pocket payment requirements for transport and treatment
options.D: High salaries paid to primary healthcare workers

explanation: When families have to pay cash right on the spot for fuel or treatment, lack of money can sadly cause dangerous delays. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h7)

question: How do strong cultural preferences for traditional birth attendants usually affect postnatal referrals?

options.A: They ensure all newborn red flags are diagnosed early
options.B: They often cause dangerous delays in seeking formal medical care
options.C: They train primary health nurses in advanced surgical skills
options.D: They help finance hospital transport for emergency cases

explanation: When families trust traditional options first, it can delay them from coming to the clinic until complications become life-threatening. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T022#GNS226_U3_T022_h7)
